questions.question_text: A parallel-plate capacitor of capacitance 2 µF is being charged so that the potential difference between its plates increases at a rate of 5 × 10⁴ V/s. The displacement current in the region between the plates is:

solution.explanation: Between the plates no charge flows, but the electric flux changes. For a parallel-plate capacitor ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = ε₀A dE/dt = (ε₀A/d) dV/dt = C dV/dt, which equals the conduction current in the leads.
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero ignores Maxwell's displacement current. 2.5 × 10¹⁰ A divides dV/dt by C. 0.05 A brings in a spurious factor of ½.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In vacuum, electromagnetic waves of higher frequency travel faster than those of lower frequency.
Statement II: In an electromagnetic wave, the oscillating electric and magnetic fields are parallel to each other.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel in vacuum with the same speed c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀), whatever their frequency, so Statement I is false. E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, so Statement II is false.
steps: Statement I: speed in vacuum = c for all frequencies → false
Statement II: E ⊥ B ⊥ direction of propagation → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Dispersion (speed depending on frequency) happens in a material medium, not in vacuum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A plane electromagnetic wave travels in vacuum along the +x direction. At a certain point and instant its electric field is 6 V/m along the +y direction. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the magnetic field at that point and instant is:

solution.concept: Relation between E and B in an EM wave: B = E/c, with E × B along the direction of propagation
solution.explanation: In an EM wave E and B are in phase, so B = E/c at every point and instant. The direction of E × B gives the direction of propagation, which fixes the direction of B.
steps: E along +y, propagation along +x: ŷ × ẑ = x̂, so B is along +z
solution.why_others_wrong: −z would make E × B point along −x. 1.8 × 10⁹ T multiplies by c instead of dividing. B cannot be along x, the direction of travel: EM waves are transverse.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. The image is formed:

options.text: 10 cm in front of the mirror
30 cm in front of the mirror

solution.explanation: With distances measured from the pole and negative in front of the mirror: u = −30 cm and f = −15 cm. The object is at the centre of curvature, so the image is also at the centre of curvature.
steps: v = −30 cm → real image 30 cm in front of the mirror
m = −v/u = −1: inverted and of the same size
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 cm comes from writing 1/v = 1/f + 1/u (the lens-type sign slip). 'Behind the mirror' would be a virtual image, which a concave mirror forms only for objects inside the focus.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 30 cm in front of the mirror

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin convex lens of focal length 25 cm is placed in contact with a thin concave lens of focal length 50 cm. The power of the combination is:

solution.concept: Power of thin lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂, with P = 1/f (f in metres)
solution.explanation: A convex lens has positive power and a concave lens negative power; powers of lenses in contact add.
solution.why_others_wrong: +6 D treats the concave lens as converging. −2 D gets the sign of the result wrong. +0.02 D uses focal lengths in centimetres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A cut diamond sparkles brilliantly because light entering it undergoes multiple total internal reflections before coming out.
Reason (R): The critical angle for the diamond–air interface is very small (about 24.4°).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Diamond has a large refractive index (about 2.42), so its critical angle is small, about 24.4°. Light that enters a suitably cut diamond strikes the inner faces at angles larger than this and is totally reflected many times, coming out only from a few directions. The small critical angle is the reason for the multiple reflections, so R explains A.
steps: Most rays inside meet faces at more than 24.4° → repeated TIR
Both true, and R is the reason for A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not a separate fact here: without the small critical angle there would be no multiple total internal reflection.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following phenomena shows that light waves are transverse?

solution.concept: Polarisation as evidence of transverse waves
solution.explanation: Only a transverse wave has a direction of vibration perpendicular to its direction of travel that can be selected (polarised). Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.
steps: Interference and diffraction occur for all waves, transverse or longitudinal
Reflection occurs for waves and particles alike
Polarisation needs vibrations perpendicular to the direction of propagation → transverse
solution.why_others_wrong: Interference and diffraction prove wave nature, not the transverse character.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A prism of angle 60° produces an angle of minimum deviation of 30°. The refractive index of the material of the prism is:

solution.concept: Prism formula at minimum deviation: n = sin[(A + δm)/2]/sin(A/2)
solution.explanation: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, with r = A/2 and i = (A + δm)/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: √3 uses sin 60°/sin 30° (forgets to add δm and halve). 1/√2 inverts the ratio. 1.5 is only a typical value for glass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (instrument and adjustment) with List-II (magnifying power). Here f, f_o and f_e are focal lengths, L is the tube length and D is the least distance of distinct vision.

List-I:
A. Simple microscope, final image at the near point
B. Simple microscope, final image at infinity
C. Astronomical telescope in normal adjustment
D. Compound microscope, final image at infinity

List-II:
I. f_o/f_e
II. (L/f_o)(D/f_e)
III. D/f
IV. 1 + D/f

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: A simple microscope gives 1 + D/f with the image at the near point and D/f with the image at infinity. A telescope in normal adjustment gives f_o/f_e. A compound microscope with the final image at infinity gives m_o × m_e = (L/f_o)(D/f_e).
steps: Simple microscope, near point: m = 1 + D/f → IV
Simple microscope, infinity: m = D/f → III
Telescope, normal adjustment: m = f_o/f_e → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The usual slip is swapping the two simple-microscope cases: the extra '1 +' appears only when the image is at the near point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A tank contains a 20 cm deep layer of water (refractive index 4/3) with a 12 cm thick layer of oil (refractive index 1.5) floating on it. Viewed from directly above, the bottom of the tank appears to be at a depth below the top surface of the oil of:

solution.concept: Apparent depth for near-normal viewing: each layer contributes (real thickness)/n
solution.explanation: For viewing along the normal, a layer of thickness t and refractive index n appears to have thickness t/n. The apparent depths of successive layers add.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 cm treats both layers as water. 21.3 cm treats both as oil. 9 cm is the apparent shift (32 − 23), not the apparent depth.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin biconvex lens of glass (refractive index 1.5) has both radii of curvature equal to 20 cm. When it is completely immersed in water (refractive index 4/3), its focal length becomes:

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula with a surrounding medium: 1/f = (n_lens/n_medium − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
solution.explanation: Bending at each surface depends on the refractive index of the glass relative to the medium around it. In water this relative index is much closer to 1, so the lens becomes much weaker.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm is the focal length in air. 26.7 cm multiplies the air value by 4/3. 40 cm doubles it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the slits are 0.5 mm apart, the screen is 1 m away and light of wavelength 600 nm (in air) is used. If the entire apparatus is immersed in water of refractive index 4/3, the fringe width becomes:

solution.concept: Fringe width β = λD/d, with the wavelength in the medium
solution.explanation: In water the frequency is unchanged but the wavelength falls to λ/n, so the fringe width falls by the same factor.
steps: In water: λ' = λ/n, so β' = β/n
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.2 mm is the fringe width in air. 1.6 mm multiplies by n instead of dividing. 0.6 mm halves the air value.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 500 nm falls normally on a single slit of width 0.1 mm. The diffraction pattern is observed on a screen 2 m away. The linear width of the central maximum is:

solution.concept: Single-slit diffraction: first minima at a sin θ = ±λ
solution.explanation: The central maximum extends between the first minima on either side, at angles ±λ/a for small angles.
steps: Distance of first minimum from centre = Dθ = 2 × 5 × 10⁻³ = 1 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 cm is the distance from the centre to the first minimum (half-width). 4 cm doubles again. 0.5 cm uses the half-width with D = 1 m.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction at a single slit

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through two polaroids whose pass axes are inclined at 60° to each other. The intensity of the light coming out of the second polaroid is:

solution.concept: Malus' law: I = I₁ cos² θ
solution.explanation: The first polaroid passes half the intensity of unpolarised light, whatever its orientation. The second follows Malus' law with θ = 60°.
steps: After the first polaroid: I₁ = I₀/2
After the second: I₂ = (I₀/2) cos² 60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8
solution.why_others_wrong: I₀/4 applies cos² 60° to I₀ directly, forgetting the first halving. 3I₀/8 uses sin² 60°. I₀/2 stops after the first polaroid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When light is incident on a transparent medium at Brewster's angle, the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other.
Statement II: When unpolarised light is incident at Brewster's angle, the refracted light is completely plane polarised.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Polarisation by reflection: Brewster's law, tan i_B = n
solution.explanation: At Brewster's angle the reflected ray is completely polarised and is perpendicular to the refracted ray (i_B + r = 90°), so Statement I is true. The refracted light is only partially polarised, because it still contains most of both components; Statement II is false.
steps: tan i_B = n with Snell's law gives sin r = cos i_B → r + i_B = 90° → I true
Only the reflected light is fully polarised; the transmitted light is partially polarised → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II attributes to the refracted beam what is true only of the reflected beam.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation by reflection
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In Young's double-slit experiment performed with white light, the central fringe is coloured.
Statement II: Two independent sodium lamps cannot act as coherent sources, because the phase difference between the light from them changes rapidly and randomly with time.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Interference with white light; coherent sources
solution.explanation: At the centre the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all colours interfere constructively and the central fringe is white (Statement I false). Light from independent sources has a phase difference that changes randomly in about 10⁻¹⁰ s, so the pattern averages out; they are incoherent (Statement II true).
steps: Path difference zero at centre for all λ → bright for all colours → white → I false
Independent sources: random phase changes → incoherent → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: The fringes on either side of the centre are coloured, which is where the idea of a coloured central fringe comes from.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', coherent and incoherent addition of waves; interference
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (observation) with List-II (phenomenon mainly responsible).

List-I:
A. Light guided along a bent optical fibre
B. Bright and dark fringes in Young's double-slit experiment
C. Light spreading into the geometrical shadow behind a narrow slit
D. Polaroid sunglasses cutting down glare

List-II:
I. Diffraction
II. Polarisation
III. Total internal reflection
IV. Interference

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Optical fibres trap light by repeated total internal reflection; Young's fringes come from superposition of two coherent waves; bending into the shadow is diffraction; polaroids block one plane of vibration.
steps: Optical fibre → total internal reflection → III
Spreading behind a slit → diffraction → I
solution.why_others_wrong: Interference and diffraction are often swapped: two coherent sources give interference; bending at one narrow opening is diffraction.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A convex lens made of glass of refractive index 1.5 converges light whatever medium it is placed in.
Reason (R): The focal length of a lens depends on the refractive index of its material relative to the surrounding medium.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula with a surrounding medium
solution.explanation: By the lens maker's formula, 1/f = (n_lens/n_medium − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂), so R is true. If the medium is optically denser than the glass (for example carbon disulphide, n ≈ 1.63), n_lens/n_medium < 1, f becomes negative and the biconvex lens diverges light. So A is false.
steps: In a medium with n > 1.5: (n_lens/n_medium − 1) < 0 → f < 0 → diverging → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is true only when the surrounding medium is optically rarer than the glass, as with air or water.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens: lens maker's formula
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object and a screen are fixed 100 cm apart. A convex lens placed between them forms a sharp image on the screen at two positions of the lens that are 20 cm apart. The focal length of the lens is:

solution.explanation: By the reversibility of light, the two positions are symmetric: in one, the object distance equals the image distance of the other. So u + v = D and v − u = d.
steps: u + v = 100 and v − u = 20 → u = 40 cm, v = 60 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 cm is D/4, the largest focal length for which an image can be formed at all. 26 cm adds d² instead of subtracting it. 20 cm takes the displacement itself as f.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. An object is placed 1.25 cm in front of the objective, and the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision, 25 cm. The magnitude of the magnifying power of the microscope is:

solution.concept: Compound microscope: m = m_o × m_e, with m_e = 1 + D/f_e for the final image at the near point
solution.explanation: The objective forms a real, magnified image; the eyepiece acts as a simple microscope on this image.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 uses m_e = D/f_e, which is for the final image at infinity. 30 takes m_o as v/f_o = 5. 6 is the eyepiece magnification alone.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light falls normally on one face of a prism of angle 30° made of glass of refractive index √2. The angle through which the ray is deviated by the prism is:

solution.concept: Refraction through a prism: r₁ + r₂ = A and δ = i + e − A
solution.explanation: At normal incidence the ray enters undeviated (i = r₁ = 0), so it meets the second face at r₂ = A = 30°.
steps: At the second face: sin e = n sin r₂ = √2 × ½ = 1/√2 → e = 45°
solution.why_others_wrong: 45° is the angle of emergence, not the deviation. 12.4° uses the thin-prism formula δ = (n − 1)A, which is not valid for a 30° prism at normal incidence. 30° is the prism angle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the intensities of light from the two slits at the screen are in the ratio 4 : 9. The ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity in the interference pattern is:

solution.concept: Interference of waves of unequal amplitude: I_max ∝ (a₁ + a₂)², I_min ∝ (a₁ − a₂)²
solution.explanation: Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so first convert the intensity ratio to an amplitude ratio.
solution.why_others_wrong: 169 : 25 adds and subtracts the intensities instead of the amplitudes. 9 : 4 is just the ratio of the source intensities. 5 : 1 forgets to square the amplitude sums.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the refraction of light are correct?

(a) When light passes from a denser to a rarer medium, the angle of refraction is greater than the angle of incidence.
(b) When light passes from air into glass, its wavelength decreases.
(c) When light passes from air into glass, its frequency decreases.
(d) Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from air into water.
(e) The speed of light in glass is less than its speed in air.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Refraction: Snell's law and what changes at a boundary
solution.explanation: Frequency is set by the source and does not change on refraction. In a denser medium the speed falls (v = c/n), so the wavelength λ = v/f falls too. Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a rarer medium.
steps: (a) True: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r with n₁ > n₂ gives r > i
(d) False: TIR needs denser → rarer; air → water is rarer → denser
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) is the classic trap: the colour (frequency) of light does not change on entering glass. (d) reverses the condition for total internal reflection.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction; total internal reflection

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about diffraction at a single slit and about polaroids are correct?

(a) The intensity of the secondary maxima decreases as their order increases.
(b) The first minimum of the pattern occurs at an angle θ given by a sin θ = λ/2, where a is the slit width.
(c) The central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum.
(d) Increasing the width of the slit makes the central maximum wider.
(e) Polaroids can be used to control the intensity of light, for example in sunglasses and window panes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Single-slit diffraction pattern; uses of polaroids
solution.explanation: The first minima are at a sin θ = ±λ, so the central maximum has angular width 2λ/a, twice that of the secondary maxima, and it narrows when the slit is widened. Secondary maxima get progressively weaker. A polaroid transmits only one plane of vibration, so turning it controls the transmitted intensity.
steps: (a) True: secondary maxima fade with order
(b) False: first minimum at a sin θ = λ
(c) True: central width 2λ/a vs λ/a for the others
(e) True: polaroids in sunglasses, window panes and photographic filters
solution.why_others_wrong: (b) uses the condition for a path difference of half a wavelength between the edges, which is not a minimum. (d) inverts the dependence on slit width.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction at a single slit; polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The energy of a photon of wavelength 620 nm is (take hc = 1240 eV nm):

solution.explanation: With hc expressed in eV nm, dividing by the wavelength in nm gives the energy directly in eV.
steps: E = hc/λ = 1240 eV nm / 620 nm = 2 eV
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 eV inverts the formula (λ/hc). 20 eV and 0.2 eV are slips of a factor of 10 in the division.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: An electron, initially at rest, is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Using λ = 1.227/√V nm, its de Broglie wavelength is about:

solution.concept: de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through V volts
solution.explanation: The electron gains kinetic energy eV, so p = √(2meV) and λ = h/p = h/√(2meV) = 1.227/√V nm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.227 nm forgets to divide by √V. 0.0123 nm divides by V instead of √V. 12.27 nm multiplies by √V.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: In a photoelectric experiment, the intensity of the incident light is increased while its frequency (above the threshold) is kept the same. Which of the following increases?

options.text: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons
The threshold frequency of the metal

solution.concept: Effect of intensity on photoelectric emission
solution.explanation: Greater intensity at a fixed frequency means more photons per second, so more electrons are emitted per second and the saturation current rises. Each photon still has the same energy hν, so the maximum kinetic energy and the stopping potential do not change.
steps: Number of photons per second ∝ intensity → saturation current ∝ intensity
K_max = hν − φ₀: unchanged at fixed ν → stopping potential unchanged
Threshold frequency depends only on the metal
solution.why_others_wrong: Maximum kinetic energy and stopping potential depend on frequency, not intensity. The threshold frequency is a property of the metal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', effect of intensity of light on photocurrent
solution.final_answer: Option B: The saturation photoelectric current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 310 nm falls on a metal surface whose work function is 2.0 eV. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the stopping potential is:

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation: eV₀ = hν − φ₀
solution.explanation: The stopping potential is the reverse potential that just stops the fastest photoelectrons, so eV₀ = K_max.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 V uses the photon energy without subtracting the work function. 6 V adds the work function. 1 V halves K_max.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The threshold frequency for photoelectric emission is the same for all metals.
Statement II: The stopping potential depends on the work function of the metal but not on the frequency of the incident light.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The threshold frequency ν₀ = φ₀/h depends on the work function, which differs from metal to metal, so Statement I is false. From eV₀ = hν − φ₀, the stopping potential depends on both the frequency of light and the work function, so Statement II is false.
steps: ν₀ = φ₀/h, different for different metals → I false
V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ₀/e: increases linearly with ν → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is half right: V₀ does depend on φ₀, but it also rises with frequency.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', effect of frequency of incident radiation on stopping potential
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: A proton and an alpha particle, both initially at rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to that of the alpha particle (λ_p : λ_α) is:

solution.concept: de Broglie wavelength after acceleration: λ = h/√(2mqV)
solution.explanation: Through the same V, each particle gains K = qV, so the momentum is √(2mqV) and λ ∝ 1/√(mq).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 1 is the answer for equal kinetic energies (charge ignored). √2 : 1 uses only the charge ratio. 1 : 2√2 inverts the ratio.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Photoelectric emission begins practically instantaneously (within about 10⁻⁹ s) after light falls on the metal, even when the light is very dim.
Reason (R): The energy of a photon is proportional to the intensity of the light.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Photon picture of the photoelectric effect
solution.explanation: A is an experimental fact explained by the photon picture: a single photon gives all its energy hν to a single electron at once, so there is no time needed to accumulate energy. R is false: a photon's energy is hν and depends only on frequency; the intensity decides how many photons arrive per second.
steps: A true: no observable time lag, even at low intensity
R false: E = hν, independent of intensity
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A and B accept R, which mixes up photon energy with photon number.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', photoelectric effect; Einstein's photoelectric equation
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: When a metal surface is illuminated with light of wavelength λ, the stopping potential is 3.0 V. When it is illuminated with light of wavelength 2λ, the stopping potential is 0.5 V. The work function of the metal is:

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation for two wavelengths
solution.explanation: Write eV₀ = hc/λ − φ₀ for both cases; doubling the wavelength halves the photon energy. Two equations give both the photon energy and the work function.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5 eV is the photon energy at 2λ, 5.0 eV the photon energy at λ, and 0.5 eV the second stopping potential; none of them is the work function.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: A laser emits light of wavelength 660 nm with a power of 3 mW. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the number of photons it emits per second is:

solution.explanation: The beam's power is the energy carried per second, and each photon carries hc/λ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 × 10¹⁹ takes 3 mW as 3 W. 1 × 10¹³ takes it as 3 µW. 3 × 10¹⁶ takes the photon energy as 1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, dropping the factor 3 from c.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases linearly with the frequency of the incident light.
(b) The slope of the graph of stopping potential against frequency is h/e, the same for all metals.
(c) Below the threshold frequency, photoelectrons are emitted if the light is intense enough.
(d) A proton and an electron that have the same de Broglie wavelength have the same momentum.
(e) The de Broglie wavelength of a particle does not depend on its speed.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Photoelectric equation and de Broglie relation
solution.explanation: K_max = hν − φ₀ is a straight line in ν (not a proportionality), and eV₀ = hν − φ₀ gives a slope h/e for every metal. Below ν₀ no electron gets enough energy from one photon, however many photons arrive. λ = h/p, so equal λ means equal momentum, and λ changes with speed.
steps: (c) False: no emission below ν₀ at any intensity
(d) True: λ = h/p → same λ, same p
(e) False: λ = h/(mv) falls as speed rises
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) is the classical-wave expectation that the photoelectric effect disproves. (e) ignores p = mv.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation; wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model, the energy of the hydrogen atom in its nth state is −13.6/n² eV. The energy needed to remove the electron from a hydrogen atom in its first excited state is:

solution.concept: Energy levels of hydrogen; ionisation from an excited state
solution.explanation: The first excited state is n = 2. Removing the electron means taking it to n = ∞, where its energy is zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: 13.6 eV is the ionisation energy from the ground state. 10.2 eV is the excitation energy from n = 1 to n = 2. 6.8 eV divides 13.6 by n instead of n².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The radius of a nucleus of mass number A is R = R₀A^(1/3), with R₀ = 1.2 fm. The radius of a nucleus with A = 125 is:

solution.concept: Size of the nucleus: R = R₀A^(1/3)
solution.explanation: Nuclear volume is proportional to A, so the radius grows as the cube root of A.
solution.why_others_wrong: 150 fm multiplies by A itself. 13.4 fm uses the square root of A. 0.24 fm divides R₀ by 5.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, most of the alpha particles passed through the gold foil without any appreciable deflection. This observation shows that:

options.text: the positive charge of an atom is spread uniformly over the atom
electrons revolve in fixed circular orbits
most of the space inside an atom is empty

solution.explanation: If the alpha particles meet nothing massive or highly charged on most paths, the atom must be mostly empty space. The rare large-angle deflections showed that the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
steps: Most particles undeflected → most of the atom is empty space
A few deflected by large angles → tiny, massive, positively charged nucleus
solution.why_others_wrong: A uniform spread of positive charge (Thomson's model) cannot produce the rare large-angle scattering. The experiment says nothing about electron orbits or neutrons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', alpha-particle scattering and Rutherford's nuclear model of atom
solution.final_answer: Option D: most of the space inside an atom is empty

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The mass defect of a certain nucleus is 0.02 u. Taking 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², its binding energy is:

solution.explanation: The binding energy is the energy equivalent of the mass defect.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.863 MeV and 186.3 MeV misplace the decimal point. 9.315 MeV halves the result.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The ratio of the wavelength of the first line of the Lyman series to that of the first line of the Balmer series of hydrogen is:

solution.explanation: The first line of a series is the transition from the next higher level: 2 → 1 for Lyman and 3 → 2 for Balmer.
solution.why_others_wrong: 27 : 5 is the inverse ratio (energies, not wavelengths). 3 : 4 and 4 : 9 compare only parts of the two brackets.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom is 0.53 Å. The radius of the orbit with n = 3 in a singly ionised helium ion (He⁺, Z = 2) is:

solution.concept: Bohr radius for hydrogen-like ions: r_n = 0.53 n²/Z Å
solution.explanation: The radius grows as n² and shrinks as 1/Z because the larger nuclear charge pulls the electron closer.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.77 Å ignores Z. 1.59 Å uses n instead of n² and ignores Z. 0.795 Å uses n/Z instead of n²/Z.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom are correct?

(a) The lines of the Lyman series lie in the ultraviolet region.
(b) In a stationary orbit, the angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of h/2π.
(c) The total energy of the electron in the nth orbit is −13.6/n² eV.
(d) The speed of the electron in its orbit increases as n increases.
(e) An electron in a stationary orbit radiates energy continuously.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Bohr postulated that the electron moves in certain stationary orbits without radiating, with L = nh/2π. It radiates only when it jumps between orbits. In these orbits r ∝ n², v ∝ 1/n and E = −13.6/n² eV. Transitions to n = 1 (Lyman series) have the largest energies and lie in the ultraviolet.
steps: (a) True: Lyman series in the ultraviolet
(d) False: v_n ∝ 1/n, so speed falls as n rises
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) is what classical physics predicts and Bohr's postulate denies. (d) reverses v ∝ 1/n.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom; the line spectra of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The density of nuclear matter is nearly the same for all nuclei.
Statement II: The nuclear force between two nucleons is nearly independent of their charge and acts only over very short distances, of the order of a few femtometres.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Nuclear density and the nuclear force
solution.explanation: Since R = R₀A^(1/3), the nuclear volume is proportional to A and so is the mass; the density is therefore nearly the same (about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) for all nuclei. The nuclear force is short-ranged and nearly the same for n–n, n–p and p–p pairs.
steps: Volume ∝ R³ ∝ A and mass ∝ A → density independent of A → I true
Nuclear force: short range, charge independent → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are standard NCERT facts; neither is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', size of the nucleus; nuclear force
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I:
A. Nuclear fission
B. Nuclear fusion
C. Mass defect
D. Maximum binding energy per nucleon

List-II:
I. Nuclei near A = 56 (iron)
II. Main source of the Sun's energy
III. Basis of the energy produced in a nuclear reactor
IV. Difference between the total mass of the free nucleons and the mass of the nucleus

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Reactors use controlled fission of heavy nuclei. The Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium. The mass defect is the mass that disappears when nucleons bind. Binding energy per nucleon peaks (about 8.75 MeV) near A = 56.
steps: Fusion → energy of the Sun → II
Mass defect → Σ(nucleon masses) − nuclear mass → IV
Peak of B/A curve → A ≈ 56 → I
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping fission and fusion is the usual slip: reactors use fission; stars use fusion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass–energy and nuclear binding energy; nuclear energy
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A nucleus of mass number 240, with a binding energy of 7.6 MeV per nucleon, splits into two nuclei of mass number 120 each, with a binding energy of 8.5 MeV per nucleon. The energy released in the process is:

solution.concept: Energy released = (total binding energy of products) − (total binding energy of the parent)
solution.explanation: Energy is released because the products are more tightly bound; the gain in binding energy appears as kinetic energy of the fragments.
solution.shortcut: Total nucleon number is unchanged, so Q = 240 × (8.5 − 7.6) = 216 MeV.
solution.why_others_wrong: 108 MeV counts only one fragment. 0.9 MeV is the gain per nucleon. 432 MeV counts the gain twice.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An alpha particle with a kinetic energy of 5 MeV is directed head-on at a gold nucleus (Z = 79). Taking e²/(4πε₀) = 1.44 MeV fm, the distance of closest approach is about:

solution.explanation: In a head-on approach the alpha particle stops momentarily when all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy (the heavy gold nucleus is taken as fixed).
solution.why_others_wrong: 22.8 fm takes the alpha particle's charge as e instead of 2e. 91.0 fm doubles once more. 4.55 fm is a decimal slip.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', alpha-particle trajectory; distance of closest approach

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Photons emitted when hydrogen atoms make the transition from n = 4 to n = 2 fall on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. Taking E_n = −13.6/n² eV, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is:

solution.concept: Hydrogen spectrum combined with Einstein's photoelectric equation
solution.explanation: The photon energy equals the difference of the two energy levels. Subtract the work function to get K_max.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.55 eV forgets the work function. 10.75 eV uses the 4 → 1 transition (12.75 eV). 0.85 eV is the magnitude of the n = 4 energy, not a transition energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Energy is released both in the fusion of very light nuclei and in the fission of very heavy nuclei.
Reason (R): The binding energy per nucleon is smaller for very light nuclei and for very heavy nuclei than for nuclei of intermediate mass number.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Binding energy curve and nuclear energy
solution.explanation: B/A is low for light nuclei, rises to about 8.75 MeV near A = 56 and falls to about 7.6 MeV at A = 238 (this is R, which is true). Fusing light nuclei or splitting a heavy nucleus gives products with higher B/A, that is, more tightly bound, and the extra binding energy is released (A, true). So R explains A.
steps: R true: shape of the B/A versus A curve
A true: fusion and fission both move towards higher B/A
Higher B/A of the products is why energy is released → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Option B is the trap: R is not merely related; the binding energy curve is exactly why both processes release energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass–energy and nuclear binding energy
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following impurities, when added in small amounts to pure silicon, makes it a p-type semiconductor?

solution.explanation: A trivalent atom such as boron, aluminium or indium has only three valence electrons, so one bond with neighbouring silicon atoms is incomplete. This creates a hole, making holes the majority carriers.
steps: Trivalent dopant (B, Al, Ga, In) → acceptor → p-type
Pentavalent dopant (As, P, Sb) → donor → n-type
solution.why_others_wrong: Arsenic, phosphorus and antimony are pentavalent donors, which make n-type silicon.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A full-wave rectifier is supplied with a 50 Hz AC input. The fundamental frequency of the ripple in its output is:

solution.explanation: A full-wave rectifier sends current through the load in the same direction in both halves of each input cycle, so the output has two pulses per input cycle.
steps: Output: 2 pulses per input cycle → 100 pulses per second → 100 Hz
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 Hz is the ripple frequency of a half-wave rectifier. 25 Hz halves instead of doubling. 200 Hz doubles twice.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', application of junction diode as a rectifier

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A two-input logic gate gives an output 0 only when both its inputs are 1, and an output 1 for every other combination of inputs. The gate is:

solution.concept: Truth tables of basic logic gates
solution.explanation: Y = 0 only for A = B = 1 is the opposite of AND (which gives 1 only for A = B = 1). This is the NAND gate, Y = (A·B)'.
steps: AND: Y = 1 only when A = B = 1
NAND = NOT(AND): Y = 0 only when A = B = 1
NOR: Y = 1 only when A = B = 0; OR: Y = 0 only when A = B = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: AND has the opposite outputs. NOR gives 1 only for both inputs 0. OR gives 0 only for both inputs 0.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A silicon crystal has an intrinsic carrier concentration of 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³. It is doped so that the electron concentration becomes 4.5 × 10²² m⁻³. In thermal equilibrium, the hole concentration is:

solution.explanation: Doping raises one carrier concentration and, by recombination, lowers the other, keeping the product equal to n_i².
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³ is the intrinsic value, which applies only before doping. 4.5 × 10²² m⁻³ assumes equal numbers of holes and electrons. 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ m⁻³ divides n_i by n_e without squaring.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode with a breakdown voltage of 6 V is used as a voltage regulator. It is connected through a 200 Ω series resistor to a 10 V DC supply, and a 1 kΩ load resistor is connected across the Zener diode. The current through the Zener diode is:

solution.concept: Zener regulator: current division between Zener and load
solution.explanation: In breakdown the Zener holds 6 V across itself and the load. The series resistor drops the rest of the supply voltage and carries the total current, which splits between the load and the Zener.
steps: Voltage across series resistor = 10 − 6 = 4 V → I_s = 4/200 = 20 mA
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 mA is the current in the series resistor. 6 mA is the load current. 26 mA adds the load current instead of subtracting it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode as a voltage regulator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Inputs A and B are each passed through a NOT gate, and the two outputs are fed to an AND gate. The circuit as a whole behaves as:

solution.explanation: The output is Y = A'·B'. By De Morgan's theorem A'·B' = (A + B)', which is the NOR function.
steps: Output 1 only for both inputs 0 → NOR
solution.why_others_wrong: NAND would be A' + B' (inverted inputs into an OR gate). OR and AND have different truth tables.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a p-n junction is forward biased, the width of its depletion region decreases.
Statement II: The small current in a reverse-biased p-n junction diode is due to the majority charge carriers.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Forward bias opposes the built-in potential, lowering the barrier and narrowing the depletion region (Statement I true). In reverse bias the barrier rises, majority carriers cannot cross, and the small current (of the order of µA) is due to minority carriers drifting across the junction (Statement II false).
steps: Forward bias: barrier height and depletion width decrease → I true
Reverse current: drift of minority carriers → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Majority carriers produce the large forward current, not the small reverse current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction under forward and reverse bias
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A photodiode is operated under reverse bias.
Reason (R): Under reverse bias, the fractional change in current caused by light is much larger than the fractional change under forward bias.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why a photodiode is reverse biased
solution.explanation: Light creates electron–hole pairs that add to the minority-carrier current. Under forward bias this extra current is tiny compared with the large majority-carrier current, so it is hard to detect. Under reverse bias the dark current is very small, so the same photocurrent is a large fraction of it. This is precisely why photodiodes are reverse biased.
steps: A true: photodiodes are used in reverse bias
R true: minority-carrier current is small, so light changes it by a large fraction
R is the reason for A → option A
solution.why_others_wrong: Option B would require R to be unrelated to A, but R is the very reason given in NCERT.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices: photodiode
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (device) with List-II (how it is operated or used).

List-I:
A. Light emitting diode
B. Photodiode
C. Solar cell
D. Zener diode in a voltage regulator

List-II:
I. Reverse biased, used to detect optical signals
II. Operated in the reverse breakdown region
III. Forward biased, emits light
IV. No external bias; generates an emf when light falls on it

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: An LED emits light when electrons and holes recombine under forward bias. A photodiode is reverse biased to detect light. A solar cell needs no bias; light generates an emf. A Zener diode regulates voltage in its reverse breakdown region.
steps: LED → forward biased, emits light → III
Photodiode → reverse biased, detects light → I
Solar cell → no external bias, generates emf → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping the photodiode and the solar cell is the usual slip: one is a detector that needs reverse bias, the other a source of emf with no bias.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', special purpose p-n junction diodes
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 6 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected in series with a 1 kΩ resistor to two parallel branches. Branch P contains an ideal diode that is forward biased by the battery, in series with a 2 kΩ resistor. Branch Q contains an ideal diode that is reverse biased by the battery, in series with a 1 kΩ resistor. The current drawn from the battery is:

solution.explanation: An ideal diode is a short circuit when forward biased and an open circuit when reverse biased. So branch Q carries no current and the circuit reduces to 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ in series.
steps: Branch Q: reverse-biased diode → open → no current
Branch P: forward-biased diode → short → 2 kΩ
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.6 mA lets both branches conduct (2 kΩ ∥ 1 kΩ in series with 1 kΩ). 3 mA lets only branch Q conduct. 1.5 mA adds all three resistors in series.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An LED has a forward voltage of 2.0 V when it carries its rated current of 20 mA. It is to be run from a 9 V DC supply through a series resistor. The resistance needed and the power dissipated in that resistor are:

solution.concept: Series resistor for an LED: R = (V_supply − V_LED)/I
solution.explanation: The LED fixes its own forward voltage; the resistor must drop the remaining voltage at the rated current.
steps: Power in resistor = I²R = (0.02)² × 350 = 0.14 W (= 7 V × 0.02 A)
solution.why_others_wrong: 450 Ω and 0.18 W ignore the LED's forward voltage. 0.04 W is the power in the LED (2 V × 20 mA), not in the resistor. 100 Ω uses the LED's voltage instead of the resistor's.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about semiconductors are correct?

(a) In an intrinsic semiconductor, the number density of free electrons equals that of holes.
(b) In a p-type semiconductor, holes are the minority carriers.
(c) Doping silicon with a trivalent impurity produces an n-type semiconductor.
(d) The energy band gap of silicon is larger than that of germanium.
(e) In an n-type semiconductor, electrons are the majority carriers, and the material as a whole is electrically neutral.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: In a pure crystal each thermally freed electron leaves one hole, so n_e = n_h. Trivalent dopants give holes (p-type), with holes as the majority carriers; pentavalent dopants give electrons (n-type). Doping adds neutral atoms, so a doped crystal stays neutral. The band gap is about 1.1 eV for Si and 0.7 eV for Ge.
steps: (b) False: holes are the majority carriers in p-type
(e) True: majority electrons, but overall neutral
solution.why_others_wrong: A common misconception is that n-type material is negatively charged; it is neutral, because every donor electron leaves behind a positive donor ion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about rectifiers and the Zener diode are correct?

(a) In a centre-tap full-wave rectifier, both diodes conduct at the same time.
(b) The output of a rectifier without a filter is a pulsating (fluctuating) DC voltage.
(c) A Zener diode is made by heavily doping both its p- and n-sides, which makes its depletion region very thin.
(d) In a half-wave rectifier, current flows through the load during only one half of each input cycle.
(e) A Zener voltage regulator keeps the output voltage nearly constant even when the input voltage changes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: In a centre-tap rectifier the two diodes conduct in alternate half-cycles. Without a filter, the output is unidirectional but pulsating. A Zener diode is heavily doped, so its depletion layer is thin and the field is strong enough for breakdown at a low, sharp voltage; in breakdown the voltage across it stays nearly constant over a wide range of current.
steps: (c) True: heavy doping, thin depletion layer
(d) True: half-wave rectifier passes one half-cycle
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (a) are wrong; the option with only (b), (d) and (e) leaves out the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', rectifier; Zener diode

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a vernier calipers, one main scale division is 1 mm and 10 vernier scale divisions coincide with 9 main scale divisions. While measuring the diameter of a rod (with no zero error), the main scale reading is 2.4 cm and the 6th vernier division coincides with a main scale division. The diameter of the rod is:

solution.concept: Vernier calipers: least count = 1 MSD − 1 VSD; reading = MSR + (VSC × LC)
solution.explanation: The least count is the difference between one main-scale and one vernier-scale division.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.406 cm takes the least count as 0.01 mm. 3.00 cm adds 6 mm instead of 6 × 0.1 mm. 2.94 cm adds 6 × 0.9 mm, the length of 6 vernier divisions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (laboratory set-up) with List-II (quantity it is used to determine).

List-I:
A. Metre bridge
B. Resonance tube
C. Steel ball falling at terminal velocity through glycerine
D. Capillary rise in a glass tube

List-II:
I. Surface tension of water
II. Speed of sound in air
III. Resistivity of the material of a wire
IV. Coefficient of viscosity of the liquid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Each set-up isolates one quantity: a metre bridge compares resistances, a resonance tube finds λ at a known frequency, terminal velocity in a viscous liquid gives η by Stokes' law, and capillary rise gives surface tension.
steps: Metre bridge → unknown resistance → resistivity ρ = RA/l → III
Resonance tube → resonating lengths → λ → v = fλ → II
Capillary rise h → S = hρgr/(2 cos θ) → I
solution.why_others_wrong: Mixing up the two fluid experiments (viscosity and surface tension) is the most likely slip.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. With the studs closed it shows a positive zero error of +0.03 mm. While measuring the diameter of a wire, the main scale reading is 3.5 mm and the 42nd circular division is on the reference line. The corrected diameter of the wire is:

solution.concept: Screw gauge: least count = pitch/number of circular divisions; true reading = observed reading − zero error
solution.explanation: A positive zero error means the gauge reads too much, so it is subtracted from every reading.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.95 mm adds the positive zero error instead of subtracting it. 3.92 mm ignores the zero error. 3.68 mm takes the least count as 0.005 mm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the simple pendulum experiment, the time for 20 or more oscillations is measured rather than the time for a single oscillation.
Reason (R): Timing many oscillations reduces the least count of the stop-watch.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: The least count of a stop-watch is fixed by its design (for example 0.1 s) and the reaction-time error at start and stop is about the same however long the timing is. Spreading this fixed error over 20 periods makes the error in one period, and the percentage error, 20 times smaller. So A is true and R is false.
steps: A true: standard practice for the pendulum experiment
R false: the least count does not change; the percentage error in T falls
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A and B accept R; the least count is a property of the instrument, not of the measurement.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the u–v method for finding the focal length of a concave mirror, a graph of 1/v against 1/u (magnitudes) is a straight line that cuts both axes at 1/f.
Statement II: In the experiment to plot the i–δ curve of a prism, the angle of deviation first decreases and then increases as the angle of incidence is increased.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: For a real image formed by a concave mirror, 1/|v| + 1/|u| = 1/|f|, a straight line of slope −1 with both intercepts equal to 1/|f| (Statement I true). For a prism, δ falls to a minimum (δm) at one angle of incidence and rises again on either side (Statement II true).
steps: 1/|v| = −1/|u| + 1/|f| → straight line, intercepts 1/f on both axes → I true
i–δ curve: δ decreases, reaches δm, then increases → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither statement is false; a graph of v against u would be a hyperbola, which is perhaps why the first statement looks doubtful.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an experiment to find the resistivity of the material of a wire using ρ = πd²R/(4L), the percentage errors in measuring the diameter d, resistance R and length L are 1%, 2% and 0.5% respectively. The maximum percentage error in ρ is:

solution.concept: Propagation of errors: for ρ = k dᵃ Rᵇ L⁻ᶜ, Δρ/ρ = a(Δd/d) + b(ΔR/R) + c(ΔL/L)
solution.explanation: Relative errors add for products and quotients, each multiplied by the power of the quantity. Errors are always added, even for quantities in the denominator.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.5% forgets the power 2 on d. 2.5% leaves out d altogether. 5.0% counts the error in L twice.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an experiment, a steel ball of diameter 2 mm (density 7800 kg/m³) falls through glycerine (density 1050 kg/m³) and reaches a terminal velocity of 5 cm/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the coefficient of viscosity of glycerine is:

solution.concept: Stokes' law at terminal velocity: v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η)
solution.explanation: At terminal velocity the weight is balanced by buoyancy plus viscous drag, 6πηrv_t = (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.15 Pa s drops the factor 2. 1.2 Pa s uses the diameter as the radius. 0.35 Pa s ignores buoyancy (uses ρ instead of ρ − σ).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many atoms in all are present in 4.4 g of carbon dioxide? (C = 12, O = 16, Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)

solution.concept: Mole concept: moles = mass / molar mass; atoms = moles of molecules × atoms per molecule × Nₐ
solution.explanation: Find the moles of CO₂ first. Each CO₂ molecule has three atoms (one C and two O).
steps: Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 g mol⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.022 × 10²² counts molecules, not atoms. 1.204 × 10²³ counts only the oxygen atoms. 1.807 × 10²⁴ treats the 4.4 g sample as one mole of CO₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (law) with List-II (scientist who proposed it).

List-I:
A. Law of conservation of mass
B. Law of definite proportions
C. Law of gaseous volumes
D. Law of multiple proportions

List-II:
I. Joseph Proust
II. Antoine Lavoisier
III. Joseph Gay-Lussac
IV. John Dalton

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Laws of chemical combination and the scientists who stated them
solution.explanation: Lavoisier stated that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Proust found that a given compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass. Gay-Lussac observed that gases combine in simple whole-number ratios by volume. Dalton proposed the law of multiple proportions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', laws of chemical combinations
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The percentage by mass of nitrogen in urea, CO(NH₂)₂, is (C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, H = 1):

solution.concept: Mass per cent of an element in a compound
solution.explanation: Mass per cent = (mass of the element in one mole of the compound / molar mass) × 100. Urea has two nitrogen atoms per molecule.
steps: Molar mass of urea = 12 + 16 + 2 × (14 + 2) = 60 g mol⁻¹
Mass of N per mole = 2 × 14 = 28 g
solution.why_others_wrong: 23.3% counts only one nitrogen atom. 26.7% is the mass per cent of oxygen and 20.0% that of carbon.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 4 g of hydrogen gas is mixed with 40 g of oxygen gas and the mixture is exploded. The maximum mass of water that can be formed is (H = 1, O = 16):

solution.explanation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Find which reactant runs out first; it alone decides how much product forms.
steps: Moles of H₂ = 4/2 = 2 mol; moles of O₂ = 40/32 = 1.25 mol
2 mol H₂ needs only 1 mol O₂, and 1.25 mol is available → H₂ is the limiting reagent
2 mol H₂ gives 2 mol H₂O = 2 × 18 = 36 g (0.25 mol O₂ is left over)
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 g takes O₂ as the limiting reagent (1.25 mol O₂ would need 2.5 mol H₂). 44 g simply adds the masses and ignores the unused oxygen. 18 g wrongly takes 2 mol H₂ to give 1 mol water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Its molar mass is 56 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is (C = 12, H = 1):

solution.concept: Empirical formula from mass per cent, then molecular formula from molar mass
solution.explanation: Divide each mass per cent by the atomic mass to get relative moles, reduce to the simplest whole-number ratio, then multiply the empirical formula by n = molar mass / empirical formula mass.
steps: Ratio C : H = 7.14 : 14.3 = 1 : 2 → empirical formula CH₂ (mass 14)
solution.why_others_wrong: CH₂ is only the empirical formula. C₂H₄ has the right ratio but a molar mass of 28. C₄H₁₀ has mass 58 and a C : H ratio of 2 : 5.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 1 g of O₂ and 1 g of O₃ contain the same number of oxygen atoms.
Reason (R): O₂ and O₃ have the same molar mass.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Moles of atoms in equal masses of allotropes
solution.explanation: Both samples are made only of oxygen atoms, so equal masses contain equal numbers of oxygen atoms: 1 g contains 1/16 mol of O atoms either way. A is true. The molar masses are different (32 and 48 g mol⁻¹), so R is false.
steps: O₂: 1/32 mol molecules × 2 = 1/16 mol O atoms
O₃: 1/48 mol molecules × 3 = 1/16 mol O atoms → A true
Molar mass of O₂ = 32 g mol⁻¹, of O₃ = 48 g mol⁻¹ → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: The numbers of molecules differ (O₂ has more molecules); only the numbers of atoms are equal.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: One mole of water contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.
Statement II: The mass of one mole of electrons is about 0.55 mg (mass of an electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: One mole of water contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules. Each molecule has three atoms, so it contains 3 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.807 × 10²⁴ atoms: Statement I is false. One mole of electrons has a mass of 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 6.022 × 10²³ = 5.49 × 10⁻⁷ kg = 0.55 mg: Statement II is true.
steps: 1 mol H₂O = Nₐ molecules = 3Nₐ atoms → Statement I false
Mass of 1 mol e⁻ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg × 6.022 × 10²³ = 5.49 × 10⁻⁷ kg ≈ 0.55 mg → Statement II true
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 25 g of a limestone sample containing 80% CaCO₃ by mass (the rest being inert, non-volatile impurities) is heated strongly until no more CO₂ is given off: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The mass of CaO formed is (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16):

solution.explanation: Only the CaCO₃ in the sample decomposes. Find its moles, then use the 1 : 1 mole ratio with CaO.
steps: Mass of CaCO₃ = 80% of 25 g = 20 g
Moles of CaO = 0.2 mol → mass = 0.2 × 56 = 11.2 g
solution.why_others_wrong: 14.0 g ignores the impurity and treats all 25 g as CaCO₃. 8.8 g is the mass of CO₂ given off. 16.2 g is the mass of the whole residue (CaO plus 5 g of impurity), not of CaO alone.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Complete combustion of 0.1 mol of a hydrocarbon gives 13.2 g of CO₂ and 5.4 g of H₂O. The molecular formula of the hydrocarbon is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.explanation: All the carbon of the hydrocarbon ends up in CO₂ and all its hydrogen in H₂O. Each H₂O carries two H atoms.
steps: Moles of CO₂ = 13.2/44 = 0.3 mol → 0.3 mol C from 0.1 mol compound → 3 C per molecule
Moles of H₂O = 5.4/18 = 0.3 mol → 0.6 mol H → 6 H per molecule
solution.why_others_wrong: C₃H₃ forgets that each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms. C₃H₈ assumes the compound is an alkane instead of using the data. CH₂ is only the empirical formula; the moles of compound fix the molecular formula.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following samples contain exactly one mole of atoms (6.022 × 10²³ atoms)? (H = 1, He = 4, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16)

(a) 12 g of carbon-12
(b) 9 g of water
(c) 4 g of helium
(d) 8 g of oxygen gas (O₂)
(e) 14 g of nitrogen gas (N₂)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Moles of atoms = moles of molecules × atoms per molecule
solution.explanation: Convert each mass to moles of the species, then multiply by the number of atoms in each species.
solution.why_others_wrong: Nitrogen gas is diatomic, so 14 g (half a mole of N₂) still gives one mole of atoms; water has three atoms per molecule, so 9 g gives 1.5 mol of atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following sets of quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) is NOT possible for an electron in an atom?

solution.explanation: l can take values 0 to (n − 1), mₗ from −l to +l, and mₛ is +½ or −½. For n = 2, l can only be 0 or 1.
steps: n = 2, l = 2: l must be less than n → not allowed
n = 2, l = 1, mₗ = 0: a 2p electron → allowed
n = 3, l = 2, mₗ = −2: a 3d electron → allowed
n = 4, l = 0, mₗ = 0: a 4s electron → allowed
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', quantum numbers
solution.final_answer: Option C: n = 2, l = 2, mₗ = +1, mₛ = +½

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ground-state electronic configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion (Z of Fe = 26) is:

solution.explanation: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². When a transition metal forms a cation, the 4s electrons are removed before the 3d electrons.
solution.why_others_wrong: [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² removes the electrons from 3d instead of 4s. [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² is neutral Fe. [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ has the right count but a wrong distribution for the ion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Using Bohr's model, the radius of the second orbit (n = 2) of the He⁺ ion is (radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen = 52.9 pm):

solution.concept: Radius of a Bohr orbit for a hydrogen-like species: rₙ = 52.9 n²/Z pm
solution.explanation: The radius grows as n² and shrinks as the nuclear charge Z grows. He⁺ has Z = 2 and one electron.
solution.why_others_wrong: 52.9 pm uses n instead of n². 211.6 pm ignores Z. 423.2 pm multiplies by Z instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', Bohr's model for hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The de Broglie wavelength of a moving particle is inversely proportional to its momentum.
Statement II: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle has a significant effect on the motion of macroscopic objects such as a cricket ball.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: de Broglie relation and the uncertainty principle
solution.explanation: λ = h/p = h/mv, so the wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum: Statement I is true. Because h is so small, the uncertainties for objects of ordinary mass are negligible; the principle matters only for microscopic particles such as electrons: Statement II is false.
steps: λ = h/mv → λ ∝ 1/p → Statement I true
Δx·Δv ≥ h/4πm: for m of about 0.1 kg the product is negligible → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', dual behaviour of matter and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ratio of the wavelength of the first line of the Balmer series to that of the first line of the Lyman series in the hydrogen spectrum is:

solution.explanation: The first line of a series is the transition from the next higher level: 3 → 2 for Balmer, 2 → 1 for Lyman. Wavelength is inversely proportional to (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²).
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 : 27 is the ratio of the wave numbers (or frequencies), the inverse of what is asked. 9 : 4 and 4 : 1 compare squares of single quantum numbers instead of energy differences.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', line spectrum of hydrogen

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Particle P has four times the mass of particle Q. Their de Broglie wavelengths are in the ratio λ_P : λ_Q = 1 : 2. The ratio of their speeds v_P : v_Q is:

solution.explanation: Rearranged, v = h/(mλ), so speed is inversely proportional to the product of mass and wavelength.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 1 inverts the answer. 1 : 8 and 8 : 1 multiply the mass ratio by the wavelength ratio instead of letting them act in opposite directions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (orbital) with List-II (numbers of radial and angular nodes).

List-I:
A. 2s
B. 3p
C. 3d
D. 4s

List-II:
I. 0 radial, 2 angular
II. 3 radial, 0 angular
III. 1 radial, 0 angular
IV. 1 radial, 1 angular

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: An orbital has (n − l − 1) radial nodes and l angular nodes, so (n − 1) nodes in all.
steps: 2s: n − l − 1 = 1 radial, l = 0 angular → III
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', shapes of atomic orbitals
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers.
(b) Pairing of electrons in orbitals of equal energy (such as the three p orbitals) does not take place until each of them has one electron.
(c) The total number of orbitals in a shell with principal quantum number n is n².
(d) A single 2p orbital can hold up to six electrons.
(e) The (n + l) value of a 4s orbital is greater than that of a 3d orbital.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Pauli exclusion principle, Hund's rule and orbital counting
solution.explanation: (a) is the Pauli exclusion principle and (b) is Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity. A shell n has n² orbitals. Any one orbital holds at most two electrons; six is the capacity of the whole 2p subshell. For 4s, n + l = 4 + 0 = 4; for 3d it is 3 + 2 = 5, which is why 4s fills first.
steps: (d) False: one orbital holds at most 2 electrons
(e) False: 4s has n + l = 4, 3d has n + l = 5
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', filling of orbitals in atoms

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The ground-state electronic configuration of copper (Z = 29) is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ and not [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s².
Reason (R): Completely filled and exactly half-filled subshells have extra stability because of their symmetrical distribution and larger exchange energy.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Stability of completely filled and half-filled subshells
solution.explanation: Moving one electron from 4s to 3d gives copper a completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell. Such subshells (and half-filled ones) are extra stable because of symmetry and larger exchange energy. R is true and is exactly why A is true.
steps: Reason: symmetry and exchange energy stabilise d¹⁰ → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', stability of completely filled and half-filled subshells
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The uncertainty in the position of an electron is 0.1 nm. The minimum uncertainty in its velocity is (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mass of electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg):

solution.concept: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: Δx · m Δv ≥ h/4π
solution.explanation: Convert Δx to metres and rearrange for the smallest Δv.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.27 × 10⁶ leaves out 4π. 1.16 × 10⁶ uses h/2π instead of h/4π. 5.79 × 10⁴ takes Δx as 1 nm.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', Heisenberg's uncertainty principle

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In a sample of hydrogen atoms, electrons are excited to the n = 5 level. When they return to the ground state by all possible routes, how many different spectral lines can appear in all, and how many of them belong to the Balmer series?

options.text: 10 lines in all, 4 of them in the Balmer series
10 lines in all, 3 of them in the Balmer series
4 lines in all, 1 of them in the Balmer series
15 lines in all, 3 of them in the Balmer series

solution.concept: Number of spectral lines from level n: n(n − 1)/2
solution.explanation: Every pair of levels from 1 to 5 gives one line. The Balmer series contains only the transitions that end on n = 2.
steps: Balmer lines end on n = 2: 5 → 2, 4 → 2, 3 → 2 → 3 lines
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 Balmer lines wrongly counts 2 → 1 (a Lyman line) or a 6 → 2 line that cannot occur here. 4 lines in all is the most one single atom can emit (n − 1), not a whole sample. 15 uses n(n + 1)/2.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 10 lines in all, 3 of them in the Balmer series

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state is 13.6 eV. The energy needed to remove the electron from the n = 2 level of the Li²⁺ ion (Z = 3) is:
